Answer: The words that most distinguish the Britannica vocabulary from the Wikipedia vocabulary (ranked by distinctiveness z-score, across the 86 matched Britannica entries / 84 matched Wikipedia articles) are:

Britannica-distinctive words (counts: Britannica / Wikipedia):
1. lime — z 4.404 — 23 / 4
2. abdomen — z 4.368 — 21 / 2
3. colour — z 4.315 — 23 / 5
4. platina — z 4.233 — 18 / 0
5. carbonate — z 4.113 — 17 / 0
6. instant — z 3.625 — 15 / 2
7. cells — z 3.513 — 15 / 3
8. till — z 3.513 — 15 / 3
9. eyes — z 3.494 — 19 / 9
10. letters — z 3.386 — 21 / 14
11. burnt — z 3.371 — 14 / 3
12. pipe — z 3.349 — 16 / 6

Source: challenge_corpus (corpus-level vocabulary comparison of all matched pairs). Scope note: counts cover only entries with an accepted match; Britannica text is noisy OCR, so counts/terms reflect that OCR. Overall vocabulary overlap is modest (frequency cosine 0.5832). For contrast, the most Wikipedia-distinctive words are century (0/302), roman (4/301), lightning (2/244), steam (4/253), erigeron (1/173), erfurt (1/173), city (6/245), fleabane (0/154), esarhaddon (1/168), william (15/354), coins (3/192), new (5/212).

Caveat: these are corpus-level aggregates; the tool does not expose per-entry IDs or scan page IDs for this view, so I cannot cite individual entry IDs here. If you want the underlying evidence for a specific word, I can look up a matched entry and read its Britannica/Wikipedia text.
